title: Why Ribeiro tastes the way it does

lede.text: Ribeiro sits where Galicia's Atlantic and Mediterranean climates meet, shielded from the ocean by mountains. This limit zone for vines makes fresh, fruity white wines.

terms.text: A wine that was held in a barrel of up to 600 litres at some point, made only from principal varieties.
A sparkling wine made only from principal varieties by the traditional method, as brut or brut nature.

chapters.title: Terraces behind the mountains
paras: Ribeiro lies in the transition zone of Galicia. The Atlantic is only 45 km to the west.
Mountain chains close the zone off on the west. They protect it from the storms that come in from the ocean.
Sea influence comes mainly along the Miño basin. It grows stronger higher up the slopes, so planting stops at about 450 m.
The zone covers nine municipalities in full, and parishes and places in others.
The terrain is rough. In many cases the rough soils and terrain all but force the land into vines.

fly.caption: Mountains on the west shield the zone from Atlantic storms, 45 km from the ocean.

fly.caption: Sea influence comes in mainly along the Miño basin.

chapters.title: Mediterranean, softened by the Atlantic
paras: The climate is temperate, with four clear seasons. It is Mediterranean in character, with an Atlantic influence. Each softens the other.
Rain is scarce from fruit set onward. Day and night differ strongly in temperature, because the climate is slightly continental.
That slows ripening. That keeps the aroma and the natural freshness.
On the Winkler scale most of Ribeiro is zone II. Cooler, less sunny sites are zone I. The lowest, sunniest sites come close to zone III.
Viticulture here is almost marginal. The fruit has some trouble ripening. Alcohol and phenolic ripeness arrive together, and the acidity stays fresh, with tartaric acid ahead of malic.
The mildew index is well below its maximum. Even so, growing here depends on constant control of the disease.

fly.label: Ribeiro
fly.caption: A big gap between day and night temperatures slows ripening.

chapters.title: Granite, made into terraces
paras: Most soils form on granite. Fewer form on metamorphic rock, and fewer still on sediments such as river terraces.
Soils on granite are sandier. Soils on metamorphic rock are loam to silt.
Chemically, the soils are strongly acid and poor in bases. They fix little phosphorus. In wide areas they are little developed, and they hold little water.
Nearly all the vineyard soil is terraced. The terraces add depth, ease the slope and help with work and sun.
Growers have farmed and improved these soils for generations, and have fertilised them heavily for a long time. They can be called man-made soils (anthropic soils).

chapters.title: Treixadura and fresh whites
paras: Only the listed grape varieties may be used. Nine white and nine red grapes are principal. Three more are secondary.
Yields are capped at 13,000 kg per hectare for the principal whites, which gives 93.6 hl. The principal reds are capped at 12,000 kg. Secondary varieties may yield more.
Wines based on principal varieties identify the zone best. The rules mark them apart from the others in production and on the label.
White grapes are the most common, and Treixadura stands out. The whites are fresh and fruity, pale yellow to golden. Most are drunk in their first or second year.
The reds run from violet red to cherry red. They are fresh, intense and balanced, and are also drunk young.
Sparkling wine has been made since the early 1980s, by the traditional method. Tostado is a sweet wine from the best grapes, dried in naturally ventilated rooms.
